color.$description: The light palette. Derived roles (surface, text, border) are references into the neutral ramp, so re-tinting the ramp re-tints every surface with it.

primary.$description: Brand accent: primary actions, links, focus rings.

secondary.$description: Brand accent: secondary actions and highlights.

accent.$description: Brand accent: supporting emphasis, distinct from primary.

semantic.$description: Status colors. Named by meaning, never by hue.

surface-sunken.$description: Background of elements that sit below the page: table stripes, inset wells.

surface-raised.$description: Background of elements that sit above the page: cards, popovers, menus.

text-muted.$description: Secondary text: captions, helper copy, placeholders.

link.$description: Links read against body text, so they follow the primary.

field.$description: A field's own surface. Distinct from `surface`, so a control reads as an inset object rather than a hole in the page, and distinct from `surface-raised`, so a card on a field is still two things.

border-strong.$description: A control's own edge: stronger than `border`, which divides content. A field has to read as a field at a glance.

on-semantic-error.$description: Text on the matching fill. A fill with no foreground cannot be read, which is what this token prevents.

on-semantic-info.$description: Text on the matching fill. A fill with no foreground cannot be read, which is what this token prevents.

disabled.$description: The fill a dead control wears: the ramp one step off the page, so a control that cannot be pressed still reads as a control.

on-disabled.$description: The ink on that fill. Dimming the control instead would dim this with it, which is how a dead button becomes an unreadable one.

spacing.$description: The spacing scale. Every gap, pad and inset is one of these steps.

font.$description: Typography: which face, how large, how heavy, and how open the tracking sits.

tracking.$description: How far the letters sit from each other. A theme has a real opinion here — the open end is what separates a plain label from a shouted one — so the ramp is tokens rather than the handful of `em` values the utilities would otherwise carry.

tighter.$description: Display type only. Enough to pull a large headline back to the measure of the body it leads.

tight.$description: A heading at reading size, where the face's own sidebearings already crowd the word.

normal.$description: Body copy and anything unlabelled. The ramp's middle is a decision, not its absence.

wide.$description: The small uppercase label that reads as a clump of strokes at text size.

wider.$description: An eyebrow or category mark set above the copy it introduces.

widest.$description: A single word carrying a whole section. Past this the word stops being a word.

leading.$description: How far the lines sit from each other.

card-title.$description: The card-title voice: the name on a card, set to be found inside a surface.

radius.$description: Corner rounding, from square to fully round.

0.$description: Gone, not merely faint. The step a rule reaches for when the element should not be painted at all.

10.$description: A ghost: present in the DOM, gone from the eye. Reserved for decoration.

20.$description: Disabled. Low enough to stop a control being pressed, high enough to keep its label readable beside live controls.

30.$description: A disabled control on a dark surface, where the same fraction reads lighter than it does on a light one.

40.$description: The dimmed step: a placeholder image, a track before it is filled, a hint of content.

50.$description: Half. The step most rules ask for, so it is the one a theme is most likely to have an opinion about.

60.$description: Muted but still read: text on a disabled field that the reader is expected to transcribe.

70.$description: Secondary content that must survive a projector or a bright room.

80.$description: A hair under full strength: the hover state of something that should feel nearly solid.

90.$description: Almost opaque. The step for a scrim that must dim what is behind it without appearing to.

100.$description: Fully shown. The default, named so a rule can say it rather than assume it.

opacity.$description: How much of a thing is shown, as a fraction. A theme owns this because the same fraction reads differently over a light surface than over a dark one, and because `disabled` is a decision about how present a dead control still looks.

breakpoint.$description: Viewport widths where layout steps change.

z-index.$description: Stacking order. Layer, never a magic number at the call site.

motion.$description: How things move and how long it takes.

button.$description: Component tokens: the decisions a theme owns for its buttons. Metrics that every theme would answer the same way are spent in the CSS instead.

weight.$description: The button's own weight. A control carries more weight than the prose around it.

tracking.$description: Label tracking. Slightly tight, because a 600-weight label in a small control needs the width back.

shadow.$description: The resting elevation. A control with no shadow sits on the page rather than in it.

shadow-hover.$description: The hovered elevation. The lift is the hover feedback; without it a pointer tells the reader nothing.

border.$description: Stroke weight. Every control and surface reads `width`, so a theme changes its edge weight in one place; the numbered steps above it are the ladder a layout reaches for when one edge needs to say more than the rest.

width.$description: The hairline every control and surface draws with.

width-2.$description: The emphasis edge: a control that must read as selected rather than merely bordered.

width-4.$description: The heavy edge. Rare on purpose — a stroke this thick is a statement, not a divider.

width-8.$description: The frame. A block drawn rather than outlined.

focus.$description: The focus ring, shared by every interactive element: buttons, links, fields, summaries and dialogs.

icon.$description: Glyph sizes, from the reader's own root rather than the element they sit in — a step has to be a jump, and an `em` step against 14px prose is 2px.

badge.$description: Component tokens: the decisions a theme owns for its badges. Metrics that every theme would answer the same way are spent in the CSS instead.

edge.$description: The stroke the badge draws around itself, so a small shape holds apart from the page. Zero leaves it a bare fill with no edge.

pill.$description: Fully round reads as a pill; false squares it into a tag.

checkbox.$description: How physical a checkbox is: one scalar driving three inset shadows. Zero is flat and drawn; higher is lit and raised.

switch.$description: How physical a switch is: one scalar driving three inset shadows. Zero is flat and drawn; higher is lit and raised.

$description: Carries a `dark` group, so this one theme answers to both modes.

avatar.$description: How big an avatar is, as the edge of the square it fills. A theme owns the ladder because the size of a face is a design decision, not a product of some other token.

sm.$description: The size for a face in a list or a comment: it reads beside its label without leading the row.

md.$description: The default: a face beside a name, or a profile header at rest.

lg.$description: A face as the subject of a page: a profile header at the top of a long column.
